module.title: Unit 7: The Easy Life: Technology, Gadgets & Future with Will
module.objective: Talk about modern gadgets, technological conveniences, and make future predictions using 'will' and 'won't'.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Technology and Gadgets in Daily Life
subModules.grammarFocus: have to, don't have to, should, shouldn't, mustn't, and expressions with like

content.summary: Welcome to the reading mission for Unit 7. In this lesson, you will read short texts about modern gadgets, helpful technology, and daily responsibilities. You will practice understanding obligations with have to, advice with should, and strict rules with mustn't.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Expressing obligation with have to and don't have to, giving advice with should and shouldn't, setting rules with mustn't, and describing things with expressions like look like and sound like.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Common technology terms, household chores, and words related to modern inventions.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming paragraphs for general topics and scanning specific lines to find key details about gadgets and obligations.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short A2 texts about technology and daily life.
Locate specific details such as gadget names, rules, and chores.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns with have to, should, and mustn't.

contextWarmup.prompt: Which device do most people use every day to check messages, take photos, and browse the internet?
contextWarmup.explanation: Smartphones are compact mobile gadgets used daily for communication, photos, and internet access.

rules: Use have to to talk about rules or things that are necessary. Example: I have to finish my homework before playing games.
Use don't have to when something is not necessary. Example: You don't have to wear a suit to the party.
Use should to give positive advice and shouldn't to give negative advice or light warnings. Example: You should turn off your laptop at night.
Use mustn't when something is strictly forbidden. Example: You mustn't touch the screen with wet hands.
Use expressions with like to describe similarities, such as look like, sound like, or taste like. Example: That new gadget looks like a small box.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Confusing Mustn't and Don't Have To
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often think mustn't and don't have to mean the same thing, but they have completely different meanings.
commonTrap.wrong: You don't have to touch that wire. It is very dangerous!
commonTrap.correct: You mustn't touch that wire. It is dangerous, so you are forbidden to touch it!

paragraphs: Technology changes very fast today. Most people have got a smartphone and a laptop at home. These gadgets make our lives easier, but they also bring new rules. For example, students have to turn off their phones during lessons. You mustn't use your phone when the teacher is speaking. However, you don't have to buy expensive brand-name devices to do your homework.

At home, teenagers often have chores to finish. Anna says, I have to clean my room and do the ironing on Saturdays. But she doesn't have to cook dinner because her father loves cooking. When people talk about new technology, they often use comparison expressions. That new vacuum cleaner looks like a small robot, and it sounds like a quiet cat when it cleans the living room floor.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Gadgets, Treasures, and Future Plans

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear a conversation between two friends talking about after-school plans and finding a surprise GPS box in the park. Focus on catching key details like obligations and sudden discoveries.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about daily plans and gadgets.
Identify specific details such as obligations using have to.
Notice how words link together in fast spoken English.

keyPhrases.note: Used to say that something is impossible.
Used to tell someone not to worry about something.
Used to describe physical appearance or similarity.
Used to emphasize doing something immediately.

connectedSpeech.note: The sound /v/ in have blends into /t/ in to, becoming /f/.
The words link together smoothly in fast speech.
The final consonant /k/ of look connects to the vowel at.
The /t/ in what and the /s/ in is become voiced taps or sounds.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Technology, Gadgets & Future Plans

content.summary: Practical guide on sentence structure, modals of obligation and advice, and expressions of similarity in English writing about technology and gadgets.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Expressing Obligation with Have To
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + have to / has to + base verb + object
blueprintItems.example: I have to charge my smartphone every night.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Giving Advice with Should and Shouldn't
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + should / shouldn't + base verb + object
blueprintItems.example: You should turn off your computer before sleeping.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Describing Things with Like
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + looks / sounds / tastes like + noun or noun phrase
blueprintItems.example: This new gadget looks like a small watch.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use capital letters at the beginning of sentences and for proper names of specific tech brands or devices.
mechanicsRules.badExample: apple launched a new iphone in march.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Apple launched a new iPhone in March.
mechanicsRules.why: Apple and iPhone are proper nouns and require capitalization.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use apostrophes correctly in contractions like doesn't, don't, and shouldn't.
mechanicsRules.badExample: You shouldnt leave your charger plugged in all day.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: You shouldn't leave your charger plugged in all day.
mechanicsRules.why: The apostrophe replaces the missing letter o in should not.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not mix up have to and must when expressing rules.
mechanicsRules.badExample: You dont have to touch bare wires because it is dangerous.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: You mustn't touch bare wires because it is dangerous.
mechanicsRules.why: Mustn't expresses strict prohibition, whereas don't have to means something is not necessary.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this sentence to negative using 'don't have to':

targetAnswers: You don't have to buy a new charger today.
You do not have to buy a new charger today.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'don't have to' to express lack of obligation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite this sentence using 'should':

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite this rule using 'mustn't':
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is forbidden to use your phone during the exam.
targetAnswers: You mustn't use your phone during the exam.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Mustn't expresses strict prohibition or rules.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine these two sentences using 'because':

targetAnswers: I bought a new laptop because my old computer broke down.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Because introduces the reason for an action.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and punctuation in this sentence:

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence using 'looks like':

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this sentence into a question:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Tom has to update his software every week.
targetAnswers: Does Tom have to update his software every week?
Does Tom have to update his software every week
practicumQuestions.explanation: Questions with have to in the present simple use Do or Does.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Join the sentences using 'but':
practicumQuestions.promptText: The smartphone is very smart. It is too expensive.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'but' to show a contrast between useful and expensive.
targetAnswers: The smartphone is very smart, but it is too expensive.
The smartphone is very smart but it is too expensive.
practicumQuestions.explanation: But connects two contrasting clauses.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the error with the contraction in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: You shouldnt touch the wet screen with dirty hands.
targetAnswers: You shouldn't touch the wet screen with dirty hands.
You shouldn't touch the wet screen with dirty hands
practicumQuestions.explanation: Contractions like shouldn't require an apostrophe between n and t.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a short advice sentence using 'should' for someone whose computer is freezing:
practicumQuestions.promptText: My computer keeps freezing all the time.
targetAnswers: You should restart it.
You should restart your computer.
You should restart the computer.
You should turn it off and on again.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'should' followed by a base verb to give helpful advice.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Technology, Gadgets and Future Life

content.summary: Speaking about technology, future predictions with will, and daily routines using gadgets requires clear pronunciation of key nouns and verbs. In this unit, you will practice talking about electronic items like laptops and remote controls, giving advice with should, and discussing duties with have to.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on sentence stress when making predictions with will and stating rules with have to. Emphasize main content words such as invent, gadget, and laptop while keeping auxiliary verbs light and connected.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity
pillars.target: Clear short and long vowels in gadget and laptop
pillars.explanation: Ensure distinct vowel sounds so words are easily understood by listeners.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress
pillars.target: Emphasize main verbs and modal verbs
pillars.explanation: Stress important words like should, will, and have to while reducing helper words.

pillars.name: Connected Speech
pillars.target: Link words smoothly in everyday phrases
pillars.explanation: Connect words naturally in phrases like do the ironing and remote control.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice that the primary stress stays on the first syllable.
Keep the stress strong on the first syllable for compound nouns.
The stress remains on the second syllable across forms.
Stress both the second syllable of remote and the second syllable of control.

practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə njuːz əˈbaʊt ðə pəˈluːtɪd ˈwɔːtə wɒz ˈvɛri ˈʃɒkɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Place primary stress on the first syllable of SHOCK-ing.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice rising intonation for a yes/no question about gadgets.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ask this question with rising intonation at the end: 'Do you have a laptop?'
practicumQuestions.explanation: Raise your pitch on laptop to indicate a yes/no question.
